nodes.question: How many items have been registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)?
nodes.answer: Over 120 items have been registered with the EPA.
nodes.paragraph: Over 120 items have now been registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), including DEET as one of the ingredients, and these products are registered by around 30 distinct firms [5]. *Correspondence: S. Environmental Sciences Europe (2025) 37:36 DEET reaches the aquatic matrix due to its increased domestic usage (showering, laundry, and by other means of disposal of personal care products in the drainage channel), resulting in the contamination of the sewage channel with DEET, subsequently leading to its pres - ence in the municipal wastewater treatment plants [6]. The degradation observed in wastewater treatment pro - cedures exhibits significant variability, with reported removal rates ranging from 10 to 90% [7]. Numerous investigations have elucidated the possible neurotoxic and cardiotoxic effects associated with DEET, which can manifest as severe bradycardia, coma, encephalopa - thy, convulsions, and hypotension [8].

nodes.question: What aspect did Grazieschi et al. (2021) address in their study?
nodes.answer: Grazieschi et al. (2021) collected cradle-to-gate data from Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) to generate a database of environmental impacts for fossil fuel and bio-based insulation materials.
nodes.paragraph: However, Schulte et al. (2021) S work is lim- ited to a point-value result based on a single scenario for transportation, end-of-life and material properties. Schmidt et al. (2004a) implemented the influence of the improvement of manufacturing processes and the consequent impact at the end-of-life scenarios. Nonetheless, also in this case prod- ucts with singularly defined technical performances were investigated. Similarly, Murphy and Norton (2008) investi- gated the environmental impacts of natural fibre insulation materials, using a cradle-to-grave approach. Like Schmidt et al. Also in this case, the study was focused on specific products with defined density and thermal conductivity and did not consider biogenic carbon. There is a clear lack of generalisability for insulation products, when investigating their environmental impacts. Grazieschi et al. (2021) tried to fill the gap in the lit- erature by collecting cradle-to-gate data from Environmen- tal Product Declarations (EPDs) to generate a database of environmental impacts for fossil fuel and bio-based insula- tion materials.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What challenges are associated with using Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) for bio-based materials?
nodes.answer: The challenges include a lack of transparency and standardization, leading to uncertainties in the use of EPDs.
nodes.paragraph: The author highlighted that there is a high variance in the environmental impacts of natural materials and a limited number of EPDs. The few EPDs on bio-based materials also present significant differences in the environ - mental impacts. There are, however, uncertainties in using EPDs due to the lack of transparency and standardisation. Other studies also tried to generalise the environmental analysis of bio-based insulation materials (Cascione et al. 2022a, b, Carcassi et al. 2022) Both Cascione et al. (2022a, b) and Carcassi et al. (2022) investigated the environmen- tal impacts of novel bio-based insulation materials using Global Warming Potential (GWP100) as the main indicator. The disaggregation of GWP100 into fossil, biogenic and land use and land use change was also considered, which led to the investigation of the carbon saving potential of bio-based materials. (2022a, b) investigate the GWP100 of several bio-based materials by introducing a scenario- based LCA that considers variation in material properties, transportation scenarios and end-of-life scenarios. nodes.question: How did Hawkins et al. (2021) and Carcassi et al. (2022) approach their investigations?
nodes.answer: Hawkins et al. (2021) used Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs), while Carcassi et al. (2022) developed a Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) for small-scale material production.
nodes.paragraph: The dynamic LCIA in Carcassi et al. ( 2022 ) and Hawkins et al. ( 2021 ) demonstrated the significant potential of bio-based insulation to offset carbon emissions. Whilst both Carcassi et al. (2022) and Hawk - ins et al. (2021) demonstrated the advantages of bio-based materials, they based their work on specific products, using EPDs for Hawkins et al. (2021) and developing a Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) for a small-scale material production in Carcassi et al. (2022). Their investigation is therefore lim- ited to specific contexts. In this study the investigation of the environmental impacts is based on a case study in which the construction site is based in the UK, but it not limited to specific manu- facturer locations, and products. Product variations (density and thermal conductivity) were considered in the LCA of eleven newly commercially available bio-based insulation materials. Data on manufacturing, transportation, current and potential practise for disposal were collected from 603 The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment (2025) 30:601 620 literature to build LCIs for the studied materials.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Renewable energy certification|Environmental product declarations (epd)_qna_004
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What databases were used to gather literature for the environmental impact assessments of EHDs?
nodes.answer: The literature was gathered from three databases: PubMED, Scopus, and Embase.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Purpose There has been a recent proliferation of electronic healthcare devices (EHDs); however, their environmental impacts are not yet fully understood. EHDs have direct environmental impacts attributed to the life cycle stages including raw mate - rial extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life (EOL). In addition to the direct impacts, there are indirect impacts that arise from the use of these devices such as favourable effects on the optimization of healthcare procedures and adverse impacts arising from the additional demand for resources. Methods This critical review aimed to gain insight into the state of the art of environmental impact assessments of EHDs, after which challenges were identified and recommendations provided to move towards comprehensive environmental sustain- ability assessments. The literature review relied on three databases (PubMED, Scopus, and Embase) and specific screening steps, resulting in 17 articles, ten of which applied life cycle assessment. Results and discussion This paper identified methodological challenges in the selected studies and lack of consistency in evaluating the environmental impacts of EHDs. For example, seven studies used device-oriented FU, while others applied a treatment-oriented FU, however, all of which aim to investigate the environmental performance of EHDs.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Renewable energy certification|Environmental product declarations (epd)_qna_005
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why is it important to consider a wider boundary of the healthcare pathway when assessing EHDs?
nodes.answer: Considering a wider boundary allows for a more comprehensive environmental sustainability assessment by evaluating both the direct life cycle impacts of the device and the positive and negative effects of EHD use within the healthcare pathway.
nodes.paragraph: These inconsisten- cies between studies make it hard to understand the environmental sustainability of EHDs. Moreover, the impacts of these devices are mostly considered at the product level and overlook potential indirect impacts associated with the healthcare value delivered by the EHDs (e.g. fewer hospital bed days). Conclusions It is important to consider a wider boundary of healthcare pathway rather than the narrow boundary of the device. This will involve considering both the direct life cycle impacts of the device (e.g. impacts related to production or end-of-life) and the positive and negative effects of using the EHDs at the healthcare pathway level. This would result in comprehensive environmental sustainability assessments of EHDs from a healthcare perspective. Keywords LCA Environmental sustainability Electronic healthcare devices Electronic surgical devices Electronic non-surgical devices Healthcare pathway 1 Introduction Technological revolution has played a crucial role in dif- ferent industries such as manufacturing, financial services, retail, and healthcare sector (Lee et al. 2018). It has led to higher productivity, better customer experience, cost reduc- tion, increased efficiency, and easier communication. In the healthcare sector, technological revolution has had a pro- found impact on service delivery and quality of care.
